text: Did the courses disappear because of a computer or enrollment-system issue?

Is the "evening" itself significant to the courses disappearing?

Did the student eat the courses?

Was the student selecting food dishes (courses of a meal) at a dining hall or restaurant that evening?
Did the student cook and eat a multi-course meal that evening?
Did the student eat the food that someone else had prepared?

Was the meal a banquet or formal dinner with many courses served one after another?
Did "all of my courses were gone" mean the student ate all the courses served at the banquet?
Were the banquet's courses finished/consumed quickly because many guests were eating, so the student got none (or little)?
Was the student working/helping at the banquet (e.g., as a server) so the courses were taken away or consumed before they could eat?
Did the student attend the banquet as a guest and eat the courses?
Did someone else at the banquet take the student's food/courses (e.g., they were cleared away or taken by others)?
Were the student's courses taken away by the servers as part of the banquet being cleared/finished?
Did the student leave their seat temporarily (e.g., to go to the restroom), and when they returned, the servers had cleared away all the courses?
Did the student stay seated at the banquet table the whole time while the courses were cleared away?
Did the student fail to eat the courses quickly enough because they were distracted or busy doing something else?
Did the servers clear the courses because the student had already finished eating them?
Were the courses cleared away because the banquet's set time for each course ended, regardless of whether the student had eaten?
Was the student a slow eater, so the courses were cleared before the student could eat them?
Were the student's courses cleared away immediately after they were served, before the student had a chance to eat them?
Did the student's courses get taken away by other guests at the table rather than by servers?
Was the student's plate/bowl physically removed while they were still eating, or before they could eat that course?
Did the student eat all the courses, and "gone" means the food was gone (eaten up) — but the "no" earlier referred to something else about the banquet, not the eating?
Did the student take the food/courses home in a doggy bag or takeaway container, so the courses were gone from the table?
Were the courses cleared away between courses, with the student's own portion left untouched or the student not served their share?
Was the student blind or unable to see the food?
Did the student share a table or dining setting where plates were passed around, so the courses were taken by others before the student could take any?
Did the student's courses disappear because the student was following a special diet or rule (e.g., religious fasting) and therefore did not eat them?
Were the courses removed from the student's view because the student was wearing a blindfold or their eyes were covered (e.g., a game)?

Was the student eating at a banquet where a "course" refers to a shared dish that the student did not personally order/control, and the "courses were gone" means the shared dishes were finished by others?
Did the student actually leave the banquet early, rather than staying seated the whole time?
Was the student's food cleared away because a fire alarm or emergency evacuation occurred during the banquet?
Were the courses cleared away as part of the normal progression of the banquet (each course removed to make way for the next), so the student had eaten them before they were gone?
Is the fact that the student is a "student at HKU" (a student) an incidental detail rather than central to how the courses disappeared?
Is the word "courses" in the puzzle meant simultaneously as both academic courses and food courses (a pun where the academic framing is a decoy)?
Were the courses cleared away by the servers while the student was physically present but the student was in a state where they could not act (e.g., asleep or unconscious at the table)?
Was the student intoxicated/drunk at the banquet, so they were present but unable to eat before the courses were cleared?
Was the student a baby or very young child who could not feed themselves, so others ate/cleared the courses?
Was the student paralyzed or physically unable to move/eat, so the courses were taken away before they could eat?
Was the student a ghost or spirit who could not eat the physical food, so it was cleared away?
Were the student's hands occupied (e.g., tied up or holding something) so they could not eat before the courses were cleared?
Did the student actually eat the courses, meaning the "gone" refers to the food being gone because it was eaten (by the student), contradicting my earlier interpretation?
Were the courses cleared away only after the student had finished eating each of them, so the student did eat all courses and the "gone" is simply the natural end?
Did the student have to pre-select/order their dishes before a deadline, and because they missed or delayed, the courses were unavailable to them?
Did the student successfully pre-select the dishes before the deadline?
Did the student's pre-selected dishes fail to be served or prepared as ordered, so the student ended up with none of them?
Were the student's pre-selected dishes served but placed in front of someone else / at the wrong seat, so the student never received them?
Were the student's pre-selected dishes served to the student, but other guests at the table ate them (took from the student's plate/share) before the student could?
Were the student's pre-selected dishes served, but the student had already become full or lost appetite from earlier eating, so the courses were left/taken away untouched?
Was there a timing mismatch: the student's pre-selected dishes were served while the student was not yet at the table (e.g., arrived late), and were cleared before the student sat down?
Did the student pre-select their dishes but on the wrong date/day, so at the banquet their courses were not prepared for them and nothing was left?
Did the student attend the banquet on a different date than the one for which they had pre-selected their dishes?
Was it the servers' mistake or the kitchen's error that caused the student's courses not to reach them (e.g., wrong table, forgotten order), so nothing was left?
Did the student's pre-selection happen "before the deadline" but the courses were cancelled/removed from the menu entirely after selection (dishes discontinued)?
Was the venue/event itself cancelled after the student pre-selected dishes, so the banquet never happened / the food was gone?
Were only some of the student's selected dishes cancelled/removed while others remained?
Did the student attend the banquet without a reserved seat or place setting of their own, so the served courses were not allocated to them?
Was the banquet a formal event with pre-assigned seating, and the student sat in the wrong seat (someone else's), so the courses served to that seat's pre-ordered dishes were not the student's?

Did the student's pre-selected dishes get served and eaten by the student, but the "courses gone in one evening" refers to the student's academic course selection messing up on the same evening—i.e., two separate events told as one?
Was this a potluck or "bring your own dish" event where the student was supposed to bring courses, but the student ate them before arriving?
Did the banquet run out of food / the kitchen had insufficient courses, so the student received little or nothing despite pre-selecting?
Was the student at the banquet as a member of a performance, competition, or eating contest (e.g., a food race) rather than a normal dinner guest?
Did the student pre-select dishes but fail to pay or confirm the reservation, so the courses were not served to them at the banquet?
Did the student pre-select dishes for a banquet, but the courses served were different from what the student selected (substituted), because the student's selection was overridden?
Was the food served on a rotating table (lazy Susan) or passed around, and by the time it reached the student each course was already finished by others?
Does "course" here mean something other than a food dish or an academic class—for example, a race/golf course or a set of obstacles?
Was this a university meal-plan or dining-hall arrangement where the student selected dishes, but the meal-plan courses/food were used up or expired in a single evening?
Did the student bring/store their meal or pre-ordered food somewhere (like a fridge or shared accommodation), and roommates or others ate it that evening?
Was the food served on a conveyor belt or moving track, so the dishes/courses that passed the student were gone once they moved past (student had to grab them in time)?
Did a specific person (not the student) take or receive the student's reserved courses/food, such as a companion or a date?
Was that person the student's guest or companion, for whom the student had intentionally ordered/sacrificed their own courses?
Was that person a stranger who mistakenly received the student's dishes (e.g., a mix-up)?
Did the student voluntarily give their courses/food to that specific person (e.g., generosity, offering it)?
Was the person to whom the student gave the courses someone the student cares about, like a family member or loved one, out of love/affection?
Did the student give the courses to that person as part of a competition, dare, bet, or game?
Was the student compelled or obligated to give the courses to that person (e.g., the person was in authority, or it was a rule/etiquette requirement)?
Did the student give the courses away because the student could not or did not want to eat them (e.g., allergy, dislike, or already full)?
Did the student select the dishes by mistake or without knowing their ingredients, and only at the banquet discovered they couldn't/wouldn't eat them?
Did the student give the courses away because the student was full or had already eaten too much before their own courses arrived?
Was the reason the student gave the courses away a dietary restriction (e.g., vegetarian, religious, or health-based) that made those specific dishes unsuitable?
Did the student give the courses to that person out of charity or pity, because that person was hungry or in need?
Did the student give the courses away simply because the student disliked the taste of those specific dishes?
Had the student pre-selected the dishes on behalf of that other person (ordering for someone else), so the courses were always meant for that person and the student gave them over?
Did the student give the courses to an animal, such as a pet, rather than to another person?
Did the student give the courses away so that another person could taste/experience those dishes (sharing a food experience), rather than because the student couldn't eat them at all?
Was the banquet celebrating a specific person (e.g., a birthday or honor), so the courses had been arranged as a gift/celebration for that person, and the student gave their portions to the honoree?
Were the pre-selected courses actually assigned to that other person (e.g., by seat or reservation), so the student was simply passing the dishes to their rightful recipient each time?
Is the "specific person" someone the student was seated next to primarily because of the banquet's table/seat arrangement (a random tablemate), rather than someone the student knew?

Did the student avoid eating the courses because the dishes involved something the student found morally or viscerally unbearable to eat (e.g., live seafood or unusual delicacies), handing them to someone who enjoyed them?

The wordplay is on "courses." They are not academic classes but the successive dishes of a banquet meal, and the "deadline" is the advance-ordering deadline for that dinner. The student, a guest at a formal multi-course banquet that evening, had successfully pre-selected their dishes before the ordering cutoff. But when the meal was served, the student voluntarily passed all of their own pre-selected courses to a particular person they knew at the table, because for their own reasons the student could not or would not eat those dishes themselves. The servers then cleared the plates as the meal progressed, and the student sat in place throughout. So by the end of the single evening, every course that had been chosen/reserved for the student had been given away and taken off the table — "all of my courses were gone." The academic framing (HKU student, choosing courses before a deadline) is a decoy; the reality is a banquet where the student gave away each of their food courses to someone else, emptying their place at the table in one evening.
